items.title: Reproducing informality: return migration from social housing as constrained agency in climate-driven relocation in coastal Jakarta
items.headline: Return migration to informal housing in coastal Jakarta
bullets: Examined return migration from social housing in coastal Jakarta.
Found that people return to informal settlements due to constrained choices.
Highlights limits of climate-driven relocation programs.

plain.question: Why do people move back to informal areas after being placed in social housing?
plain.method: Studied return migration patterns in coastal Jakarta's climate relocation.
plain.finding: People return because their choices are heavily constrained.
plain.why: It shows why climate-driven relocation programs often fail to keep people.

full.explainer: This study looks at climate-driven relocation in coastal Jakarta, Indonesia. When people are moved into formal social housing, some choose to return to informal settlements. The paper investigates this return migration, describing it as an act of constrained agency. This means people are making choices, but their options are severely limited by their circumstances. Understanding why residents leave social housing to go back to informal areas helps planners see the shortcomings of current relocation strategies. It shows that simply moving people into new housing blocks does not automatically solve the challenges of climate adaptation and urban planning in the Global South, especially when social and economic needs are not fully met by the new housing arrangements.

jargon.definition: The ability to make choices, but only within very restricted and difficult options.
Settlements or economic activities that operate outside formal legal and regulatory frameworks.

full.fit: Connects to Global South urban planning, informal settlements, and the limits of formal housing interventions.

thesis.why: It provides insight into informal settlements and the human side of relocation in the Global South, offering context on housing and vulnerability.
thesis.action: Check how the study defines constrained agency in relation to settlement choices.

critical.evidence: The abstract discusses return migration to informal housing from social housing as constrained agency during climate-driven relocation.
critical.limit: The abstract does not provide empirical data on environmental risks or changes in ecosystem services.
critical.check: Look for specific push and pull factors driving residents back to informal areas.

items.title: Rethinking sustainable urban planning in the Global South: six paradigm shifts for the next decade
items.headline: Six paradigm shifts needed for Global South planning
bullets: Reviewed urban sustainability pressures across the Global South
Found current planning tools fail to match modern urban challenges
Highlights the urgent need for new planning paradigms for cities

plain.question: How can cities in the Global South handle rapid growth and climate change?
plain.method: Reviewing current urban challenges and planning failures.
plain.finding: Traditional planning tools can no longer keep up with fast urban changes.
plain.why: Vulnerable people suffer most when cities fail to plan for environmental risks.

full.explainer: Cities in the Global South are facing a crucial decade for sustainable development. Rapid urban growth, climate change, and growing social inequalities are putting immense pressure on urban systems. Environmental shocks and climate-induced migration are worsening resource shortages and expanding informal settlements. These pressures do not happen in isolation; they interact across housing, land use, infrastructure, and ecosystems, affecting areas far beyond city boundaries. Although the Global South is diverse, many cities across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East share a common problem: the speed and complexity of urban change have outgrown traditional planning institutions and tools. Despite global policy commitments, progress in implementing frameworks like the New Urban Agenda continues to lag behind what is urgently needed on the ground.
caveats: The abstract does not state the specific details of the six paradigm shifts.
Not stated how individual cities should adapt their specific planning institutions.

items.title: Urban and peri-urban agriculture in the Global South: Nexus and policies to reduce territorial inequalities and improve social welfare
items.headline: Review of urban agriculture and nexus policies in the South
bullets: Reviewed 49 papers on urban agriculture and nexus frameworks in the Global South.
Found 17 nexus types and regional differences in focus like subsistence and institutions.
Shows how integrated policies can reduce territorial inequalities and improve welfare.

plain.question: How do urban agriculture and nexus frameworks help reduce inequality and improve social welfare in the Global South?
plain.method: The authors searched a database for past studies, chose 49 relevant papers, and analyzed their themes and patterns.
plain.finding: They found 17 different nexus types and saw that southern studies focus more on structural constraints and poverty than northern ones.
plain.why: This helps cities design better policies to connect food production with social and environmental goals.

full.explainer: In many growing cities of the Global South, rapid development pushes farming out to vulnerable edge areas. Urban and peri-urban agriculture has become an important way to produce food, build social bonds, and fight climate change. However, researchers do not fully understand how interconnected nexus frameworks are used in this type of farming research or how they shape inclusive policies. To fill this gap, researchers conducted a systematic literature review using the Scopus database from 2017 to 2024. Out of 92 initial documents, 49 open-access papers met their criteria. By analyzing these papers, the study made three main discoveries. First, it found 17 different nexus categories, going far beyond traditional water, energy, and food links to include health, waste, and climate. Second, it noted regional differences: Global North studies focus on technology, while Global South studies look at survival, basic needs, and weak institutions. Third, it found that governance is often fragmented, meaning rules are local and lack broad territorial integration. Overall, the paper suggests that well-supported farming policies can reduce inequality.
caveats: The review relies only on open-access, English-language peer-reviewed articles from Scopus.
The study analyzed 49 papers out of 92 identified documents, which limits the scope.

The transition zones where urban and rural areas meet, often surrounding cities.

items.title: Indigenous communities' perceptions of ecosystem services of a montane forest ecosystem in Nigeria: Implications for restoration planning
items.headline: Local views shape forest restoration in Nigeria
bullets: Interviewed eight communities near a Nigerian forest reserve to record ecosystem services.
Found food and savannah species were ranked higher than forest conservation priorities.
Restoration must balance local livelihoods with scientific biodiversity goals.

plain.question: How do local people view the benefits provided by a protected forest ecosystem?
plain.method: Interviews, group talks, plant inventories, and botanical assessments in eight local villages.
plain.finding: Villagers recognize many benefits, but rank food and savannah plants higher than forest services.
plain.why: Restoration projects must include local needs so people support protecting the environment.

full.explainer: This paper looks at how local indigenous communities view the benefits provided by a montane forest ecosystem in Nigeria. The researchers wanted to understand how people living near a protected forest reserve use natural resources, because successful conservation must protect both wildlife and local livelihoods. By using interviews, group discussions, and plant inventories across eight nearby settlements, the study found that communities recognized anywhere from 6 to 20 different ecosystem benefits. Interestingly, people ranked provisioning services like food much higher than regulating, cultural, or supporting services. Most of these important provisioning items came from savannah plants rather than the dense forest itself. The authors suggest that landscape management should keep a mix of forest and savannah to match local needs. They also argue that restoration efforts must prioritize tangible benefits, like food and medicine, alongside wildlife conservation. Finally, because scientific goals and local priorities can clash, designing restoration plans together with local communities is essential for long-term success.
caveats: Not stated whether quantitative biodiversity metrics were tested against community perceptions.
Not stated how long the interviews lasted or the exact demographic breakdown of participants.

items.title: Evaluating ecotourism potential in arid oasis landscapes using GIS, AHP, and PROMETHEE: The Saoura Corridor case study
items.headline: Evaluating Ecotourism in Arid Oases
bullets: Used GIS, AHP, and PROMETHEE to map and prioritize ecotourism potential in an arid oasis.
Found land-use/land-cover was the most influential criterion, designating three priority poles.
Provides a transferable planning tool for drylands to balance tourism and conservation.

plain.question: How can dryland regions plan ecotourism while protecting fragile environments?
plain.method: Combined satellite data, computer maps, and math rankings to evaluate areas.
plain.finding: Identified top priority zones for development and showed land cover matters most.
plain.why: It helps guide post-petroleum regional planning in sensitive desert environments.

full.explainer: This paper looks at how to plan sustainable ecotourism in very dry, fragile oasis landscapes without damaging the environment. Looking at the Saoura corridor in Algeria, the researchers built a computer-based decision framework. They used satellite images and elevation data to model eight different environmental and logistic factors. By applying math methods like the analytic hierarchy process and PROMETHEE, they ranked 134 spatial locations. Their analysis showed that land-use and land-cover is the most important factor when deciding where ecotourism should go. The results point to Kenadsa, Béchar, and Taghit as the top priority areas for development. The authors note that this framework can be easily moved and used in other dry regions around the world, such as the Middle East, Central Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, helping regions transition away from petroleum economies while supporting global sustainability goals.
caveats: The empirical focus is limited to the Saoura corridor in southwestern Algeria.
Not stated whether economic viability beyond spatial suitability was fully tested.

items.title: Development of a Water-Retentive Hydroponic Green Roof Using Gel Beads for Sustainable Urban Cooling
items.headline: New lightweight green roof lowers temperature
bullets: Tested a lightweight hydroponic green roof prototype with gel beads using sensors.
Found a temperature drop of 1.6 to 1.7 degrees and a 6.5 percent humidity increase.

plain.question: How can we cool down cities without heavy green roofs?
plain.method: Built a small model roof using gel beads and tested it with sensors.
plain.finding: It lowered the temperature by about 1.6 to 1.7 degrees.
plain.why: It helps cool cities and makes buildings more comfortable without heavy weight.

full.explainer: As cities grow, temperatures go up and people lose natural cooling and comfort. Traditional green roofs can fix this, but they are very heavy and need a lot of maintenance. To solve these problems, this study created a new kind of green roof. It uses a lightweight material and gel beads. The researchers built a small test model and used sensors to check the temperature and humidity. Their tests showed that this new roof lowered the temperature by about 1.6 to 1.7 degrees. It also increased relative humidity by 6.5 percent. This proves that the new design can provide steady passive cooling during different testing sessions while solving the weight and maintenance issues of normal green roofs.
caveats: Only tested on a small-scale prototype
Not stated how it performs on full-scale buildings over long periods

items.title: The Synergy Between Deterministic and Neutral Processes Drives Turnover‐Dominated Beta Diversity of Non‐Volant Small Mammals in the Western Tianshan Mountains, China
items.headline: Small mammal diversity in Tianshan Mountains
bullets: Compared taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic beta diversity across gradients
Found species turnover dominated and synergy drives community assembly
Provides a practical basis for biodiversity conservation in Central Asian mountains

plain.question: What drives the differences in small mammal types across elevations in dry mountains?
plain.method: Studied small mammals across environmental gradients in the western Tianshan Mountains.
plain.finding: Species replacement across sites is the main pattern, driven by environmental and neutral factors.
plain.why: Helps us understand how mountain ecosystems work to protect biodiversity.

full.explainer: Scientists want to understand how animal communities change across different spaces and environments, known as beta diversity. This study looked at non-volant small mammals—animals that cannot fly and are not large—across the dry western Tianshan Mountains in China. They examined three angles: taxonomic (species types), functional (the roles species play), and phylogenetic (evolutionary history). The researchers found that species turnover, meaning the replacement of one species by another from place to place, was the main pattern across all three angles. Functional differences were highest among sites, followed by species and evolutionary differences. Distance in elevation was the most important factor shaping these differences. Furthermore, the analysis showed that community assembly is driven by a mix of deterministic processes, like environmental filtering, and neutral processes. As elevation distance grew, environmental filtering had less effect, while limiting similarity had more effect. These insights help explain biodiversity patterns in dry mountain regions and guide conservation efforts in Central Asia.
caveats: The study focuses specifically on non-volant small mammals in a mountain region.
Data on other animal or plant groups are not stated.
Direct links to urban planning or ecosystem services are not stated.
